prompt:
Write 10 first-person answers to the moral dilemma below for a synthetic research dataset. Each answer comes from a different fictional participant.

Dilemma:
Imagine the same warehouse case: you and another person took part in the break-in and are being questioned separately. You are shown reliable confirmation that they have already declined the deal and will remain silent. Your decision is still open. If you also stay silent, you each serve one year. If you give evidence against them, you go free and they serve five years. You will have no future contact. What would you choose? Why?

Response approach:
Weigh the main alternatives and their consequences for the people involved. Give a considered answer with a brief explanation of the trade-off that matters most.

Emotional tone:
Use an energetic, determined emotional tone about finding a constructive way forward. Direct that energy toward acting on the situation, never toward anyone's suffering.

Every response MUST include the following reasoning characteristics:
 - Concern for welfare: States that an identified person’s suffering, loss, or welfare matters to the respondent. Concern may include wanting to prevent or reduce harm and can remain present when the chosen option still harms someone.
 - Acknowledged harm: Explicitly describes the harm, loss, or distress that a particular action would cause an identified person. This records expressed comprehension of the consequence; it does not establish concern, shared emotion, or a mental-state inference.
 - Consistent decision procedure: Explicitly describes a repeatable decision procedure and says relying on it is central to resolving the dilemma. States that the same procedure would apply even when personally inconvenient; a numerical answer or bare appeal to fairness is insufficient.

No response may include the following reasoning characteristics, for any person, emotion, or time frame. Content that a description explicitly calls insufficient for that characteristic is allowed:
 - Explicit welfare disregard: Explicitly states that an identified person’s welfare does not matter or is deliberately excluded from consideration. Accepting unavoidable harm, prioritizing a competing concern, or sounding emotionally detached is insufficient.

Write each response in no more than 90 words, in ordinary conversational English. Use only the facts supplied in the dilemma; mark any uncertainty explicitly. Let the approach and tone appear through word choice and rhythm rather than by announcing them: do not open a response by stating your mood, and avoid exclamation marks. Keep the emotional expression plausible and moderate. Choose any moral position consistent with the dilemma and the assigned approach, including withholding a decision when appropriate.

Make the 10 responses distinct from one another: vary the wording, sentence structure, length, moral position, and the way the reasoning characteristics are expressed. Do not reuse openings or stock phrases across responses.

Output only a JSON array of exactly 10 strings, one participant’s answer per string. Omit numbering, headings, category names, citations, and commentary about this task.

Generation constraints:
- Express the required traits in each participant's own everyday words.
  Do not mention label names or machine keys, and do not reuse phrasing
  from the trait descriptions.
- Before writing each response, decide who the participant is and why they
  would reason this way. The required traits should follow from that
  reasoning, not be tacked on to it.
- Apply the required traits within a consistent scope: the same focal
  person, relevant emotion, and time frame.
- Keep every forbidden trait absent from every response.
- Required and forbidden traits take priority if the requested approach or
  tone would contradict them.
- Traits neither required nor forbidden are unspecified, not necessarily
  absent.
- Preserve the scenario's facts. If the required traits cannot fit the
  scenario, or cannot be expressed without a forbidden trait, return ONLY:
  INCOMPATIBLE (instead of the JSON array)
responses: Knowing they've already chosen to stay quiet changes things for me. I keep asking myself: what rule would I want to follow no matter who sits across from me? Mine is simple — don't add to someone's suffering when I have the power not to. Staying silent means we both take a year, and that's hard, but five years for them because I talked would sit heavier on me than my own sentence ever could. I'm going with silence, same as I'd choose it any day.

I think about this in terms of a rule I'd apply regardless of who benefits. If I'd condemn betrayal in someone else's shoes, I can't excuse it in mine. Five years is a long stretch for another person to carry alone, and that weighs on me. So I stay quiet. One year is a fair price for not being the reason their life gets harder. I'd make this same call even if no one ever knew what I chose.

My rule going into any decision like this: never let my comfort cost someone else years of theirs. That applies here just the same. They've already committed to silence, and testifying now would only pile five years onto their shoulders while I walk free — that image doesn't sit right. I care what happens to them even though we'll never cross paths again. One year, shared evenly, is the outcome I can live with and defend.

I keep a simple test for moments like this — would I be okay if the roles were reversed? Here, no. Speaking against them locks them up for five years while I go home, and that gap in outcomes is too stark to ignore. Their situation matters to me, stranger or not. So I stick with silence, take my year, and let the smaller, shared cost stand instead of the lopsided one.

There's a method I use before big calls: name the harm plainly, then ask if I could face the person afterward. Telling on them would mean five years added to their life just so mine stays clean — that's a real cost to a real person, and I won't pretend otherwise. I'm choosing silence, one year, because I'd apply that same check whether the stakes were low or this high.

I try to run every hard decision through one test: does this action make someone's already difficult situation worse? Testifying clearly does — it turns a shared one-year cost into a lonely five-year one for them. That gap matters to me even without ever seeing them again. So I hold to silence, accepting my share of the cost rather than shifting it onto someone whose future I have no right to make heavier.

Here's how I decide things when the outcome affects someone else's freedom: I look for the option that doesn't multiply their loss to shrink mine. Giving evidence does exactly that — five years for them, nothing for me. That imbalance bothers me regardless of what they've done. I'll take the year. It's the same call I'd make in any version of this setup, inconvenient or not.

I want to be someone whose choices don't get lighter by making someone else's life heavier. That's the standard I hold myself to consistently, deal or no deal. Speaking against them would mean walking away while they lose five years, and I can't unknow what that costs a person. Staying silent keeps the weight shared and smaller for both of us. That's what I'm doing, plainly and without hesitation.

My approach is to ask, before acting, whether I'd still choose this if I imagined myself on the other end of it. Imagining five years stacked onto someone because of my testimony makes the answer obvious. Their hardship isn't abstract to me even without further contact. So I stay quiet, take the one year, and keep the same standard I'd use in any situation where my choice could crush someone else's outcome.

I've thought this through with one steady question: is the gain worth someone else's loss? Going free while they serve five years fails that test badly — the loss is too concrete, too personal to wave off. I do care what happens to them, even as a stranger I'll never see again. So I'm choosing silence, one year each, and I'd hold to that answer under any similar pressure, not just this one.
